## Paper

## Abstract

Surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) lattices created by artificial plasmonic metasurfaces, can carry tremendous optical information and have implications for resilient and secure optical communication. However, tailoring the intensity, spectral, and spatial distributions of these SPP lattices intentionally remain challenging. Here, we develop, theoretically and experimentally, a variety of optical SPP lattices in a category of metasurface named as Kekulé metasurface. This plasmonic nanostructure localizes surface plasmonic polaritons into assorted optical lattices at the two-dimensional limit, visualized by noninvasive leakage radiation microscopy. The spatial distribution and relative intensity of the SPP lattice sites are evolved and tailored by superposing an extra wing-shaped nanoslit set. A configurable on-chip light-emitter array and high-security imaging encryption/decryption using such optical lattices are further demonstrated. This work reports a versatile Kekulé metasurface platform and well-defined SPP lattices with multiple degrees of freedoms, featuring rich physic phenomena and potential photonic elements for applications into existing technologies.

---

## Introduction

Analogous to electrons, surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs), recognized as transverse magnetic-polarized optical surface wave at the outset, have been recently casted enormous interest as quasiparticles at their most fundamental levels1–5. The quasiparticle properties of SPPs are defined by the electromagnetic field, material dielectric response function, geometry of light-matter interaction, and multiparticle scattering6. On generation, SPP quasiparticles confines in a two-dimensional (2D) metal surface, is somehow liquid-like7 and decays exponentially or into incoherent particles, varies in intensity, spectral, and spatiotemporal evolution that are otherwise accessible8. The controlled ordering of such SPP quasiparticles into demanded lattices is attractive because not only exotic but elusive multiparticle properties and quantum dynamics are uncovered but potentially it also satisfies Maxwell’s equations6 and applicable boundary conditions as required as the case for developing planar SPP amplifiers, compact radiation sources and integrated (nano) photonics devices. However, a versatile planar platform for probing macroscopic ordering and evolutions of such SPP quasiparticles is lacking, especially in 2D limit.

Herein, we demonstrate a range of highly-tunable SPP lattices based on a category of plasmonic nanostructures at optical frequency, termed as Kekulé metasurface (Fig. 1), in which patterned nanoslits in head-to-tail fashion assemble into regular hexagon nanostructures. This multivariant platform enables us to manifest the lattice type, spatial distributions, and relative intensity of lattice sites, with controllable parameters and symmetry, which has three salient features. First, most SPP lattice possesses distinguished orbital angular momentum, evolving into another SPP lattice under different combinations of helical excitation and detection lights. Secondly, the lattice topography, for example, the relative intensity of in-plane lattice sites, could be selectively cumulatively augmented by chiselling extra open nanoslits along six corner vertices acting as the outer-wings, while the shape of other lattice sites orientationally and radially smoothly evolves into blister-like lattice geometry. Thirdly, high-fidelity SPP lattices from Kekulé metasurfaces are 2D planar and maintain even under white light excitation. Here, SPP localizations are in-plane confined and presumably enable the compact integration of miniaturized plasmonic circuits with modern-day electronic circuits, differentiating from conventional 3D localization or focusing techniques, using nano-tips9–12, Fresnel lenses13, circular lenses14–16, metalenses17–19, or plasmonic Archimedean spirals20,21. As conceptual proofs, we further show that SPP lattices with amplitude-amplified sites can be principally applied as configurable on-chip light-emitting arrays and image encryptions/decryptions, enriching the metasurface family for advanced nanolasers and information security.

---

## Results

Tunable SPP lattices in Kekulé metasurface
Illuminated under circularly polarized laser, the nanoslits milled in gold film interact with the perpendicularly polarized component, and emit out intensive SPPs tailored by the geometric dimensions and orientation angles of nanoslits (please see SI Section S1)22. To be specified, as-generated SPPs stem from the superposition of co-polarized and cross-polarized fields. The extra phase shift in the latter allows the engineering of Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase (also termed as geometric-phase factor, expressed as exp(i2\alpha), where \alpha is the in-plane rotation angle of nanoslits)23. Departing from these, we develop a Kekulé metasurface via integrating such individual nanoslit (Fig. 2a) to create SPP lattices. The multiple open nanoslits are head-to-tail arranged into ‘benzene-like’ configuration with the same rotation angle (\alpha), maintaining a fixed gradient, which can convert the 2D incident circularly polarized light into a stable hexagonal lattice in the co-polarized state and customized lattices in cross-polarized state. The in-plane electric field (E||) can be expressed as follows (more detail please see SI Section S1):

E|| \propto \sum_{n=1}^{6} (\eta \sigma jE\sigma i+\eta -\sigma e-i2\sigma\alpha n jE-\sigma i)e-ik spp [xcos\theta n+ysin\theta n] (1)

where \alpha n=(n−1)l\pi/6 represents the rotation angle of n th array; l\pi/6 is the phase gradient, and l is a constant which equals to half of the lattice topology charge (TC); k spp is the wave vector of SPPs; \theta n=(n+0.5)\pi/3 denotes the angle of n th side, determining the propagating phase of SPPs; \sigma refers to different incident spin states (i.e., \sigma equals to 1 and −1, which represent left and right circularly polarized light respectively); \eta \sigma and \eta -\sigma refer to the coefficients of co-polarization order (E \sigma) and cross-polarization order (E -\sigma). Akin to the classic electron transport with a channel, liquid-like SPP propagation along the gold-dielectric interface decays because of free-electron scatterings with the polycrystal gold film. The geometric parameters of the Kekulé metasurface are optimized (see SI Fig. S2).

Equation (1) implies that several degrees of freedom (DOFs) including l, \sigma and \eta \pm\sigma, emerge for manipulating the SPP lattice in real space. For instance, when the phase gradient is zero under right circularly polarized (RCP) incidence (TC=0), we obtain a stable hexagonal SPP lattice with TC equals to 0 in left circularly polarized (LCP) state (Fig. 2b). Meanwhile, by combining with the axial (out-of-plane) electric field (Fig. 2c, see SI Section S3 for more details), meron-antimeron like lattice in normalized 3D electric field (Fig. 2d) affirms the quasiparticle characteristic of SPP lattice24. Figure 2e shows the feasible transformation of hexagonal SPP lattice into hexagonal vortex lattices (TC=1), Kagome lattices (TC=2), and honeycomb lattices (TC=3) in LCP state, at quasi-2D limit, by modulating l to be 0.5, 1, 1.5 (see SI Fig. S4), respectively. From Fig. 2a−e, we conclude that versatile SPP lattices could be manifested by Kekulé metasurfaces, enriching the lattice family and their effective control by metasurface designs (please see SI Table S1 Section S5).

To selectively engineer the SPP lattice site, we coupled the Kekulé metasurface with extra wing-shaped nanoslit sets along three high-symmetric axes passing through six corners (Fig. 2f). Combining with Eq. (1), the in-plane electric field of wing-shaped nanoslit sets in cross-polarization state can be expressed as:

E|| o, t \propto \sum_{n=1}^{6} (E||, -\sigma+ A M e-2(\alpha n+\Delta\alpha)\sigma i e-ik spp (xcos(\theta n+\Delta\theta)+ysin(\theta n+\Delta\theta)))|E-\sigma i (2)

where \Delta\alpha and \Delta\theta (herein, equals to \pi/6) are the relative values of the rotation and azimuth angle of the outer wing-shaped nanoslits to the angle (\alpha n, \theta n). A M is the factor that is affected by the number (M) of the wingsets and distance (|r i|, i=1 to 6) to the enhanced lattice site (O). Therefore, deriving from Eq. (2), the intensity of lattice sites can be selectively engineered by \Delta\alpha, M, and its relative distance (\Delta r, which equals to |r|-Rsin(\pi/3)). Figure 2g presents that the center spot (lattice site A) intensity monotonically increases with M increment and exhibits no sign of saturation for neglected SPP decay. For M=4, the in-plane electric field at hexagonal SPP lattice site A (central image, Fig. 2h) is enhanced up to 390% with respect to that of M=0 metasurface (Fig. 2b), while the intensity of surrounding lattice site B remains barely changed (normalized 3D electric field, see SI Fig. S5). The rigid shift of wing-shaped nanoslit set relative to the nanoslit hexagon along three high-symmetry axis (offsets equal to \lambda spp/sin(\pi/3), Fig. 2f) leads to remarkable intensity enhancement (~320%) of SPP lattice site B. These good correlations clearly show the custom-tailoring of the designed Kekulé metasurface over SPP lattice, which is superior to other hexagonal metasurfaces (see SI Fig. S6).

Realization and control of versatile SPP lattices
We next reproduce the SPP lattice in real space based on M=0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 Kekulé metasurfaces via finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation (Fig. 3a–e, please see Methods for more details). For M=0, lattice sites B located at the vertices of a regular hexagon is surrounding lattice site A with a quite weak secondary maximum. After incorporating wing-shaped nanoslit arrays varying M from 0 to 4, two strikable features arise: (1) the intensity of lattice site A grows linearly and increases by approximate fourfold, accompanied by an increasingly intensified ring emerging between lattice site A and B; (2) the outer lattice site B tend to evolve from regular hexagon into a ring-like pattern composed of multiple bright spots. These salient features are reminiscent of the recently reported electronic crystallization and melting behaviors in two-dimensional van der Waals heterostructures25–31. Interestingly, such evolution phenomena are also visualized for other TC Kekulé metasurfaces by adding wing-shaped nanoslit sets (see SI Fig. S6).

To validate our predictions, we fabricated a series of Kekulé metasurfaces with M varying from 0 to 4 (Fig. 3f–j, bottom panels, please also see Methods). Considering that these SPP lattices dynamically consist in-plane SPPs under strong local-field and are highly susceptible to external fluctuations, in particular a sharp metallic tip based on near-field interactions9–12,32, leakage radiation microscopy (LRM)‒a versatile optical far-field method to direct quantitative imaging and analysis of SPPs in 2D limit is adopted33. Moreover, a mask and a filter were employed for both spatially and spectrally filtering the light directly transmitted through the sample, so that only pure SPPs were collected. The observed SPP ring in Fourier space (see SI Fig. S8) proves that pure SPP modes in real space (upper panels, Fig. 3f–j) were recorded by our home-made leakage radiation microscope. Surprisingly, patterns of measured SPP lattices from M=0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 Kekulé metasurfaces consistently dovetail with experimental and simulated references. The strong regularity between the selection of extra nanoslit positions and the optical lattice field intensity is also validated (see SI Fig. S9). Yet another interesting observation is that SPP localizations at lattice site A near linearly increase with added wing-shaped nanoslit sets, by carefully examining the intensity line profiles from experimental results (Fig. 3k). These features coincide with our simulated results, and suggest the cumulative SPP localizations and instinctive information-carrier nature of SPP lattices. Besides the in-plane SPP modes, our proposed Kekulé metasurface is also suitable for enhancing the scattering field, which is experimentally verified with optical lattice distribution as middle panels in Fig. 3f–j (more experimental details, please see SI section S12). The corresponding intensity profile (Fig. 3k) similarly exhibits optical lattices and tunable intensity. To further verify the universality of our proposed wing-shaped Kekulé metasurfaces, we also demonstrate the feasibility with different sizes and different plasmonic metals (see SI Note S11). Overall, the unique combination of extra wing-shaped nanoslits and basic Kekulé metasurface offers a major boost to the field intensity enhancement both for in-plane SPPs and scattering light.

Reconfiguring on-chip light-emitting array
The achievement of high-tunable SPP lattices by an extra wing-shaped nanoslit set in our Kekulé structure is promising in various applications. For example, reconfigurable light-emitting array uses SPP lattices with different lattice sites A intensity to enable on-chip patterned light sources, to the best of our knowledge, which has barely been reported before34,35. Kekulé metasurfaces with M=0 and M=4 were configured into array on a single chip, as sketched in Fig. 4a. Multiple M=4 Kekulé structures were assembled into ‘N-U-A-A’ letters while the rest sites were occupied by M=0 Kekulé structures. The ‘N’ and ‘U’ letters consist of ten M=4 structures while ‘A’ letter is composed of twelve M=4 structures. By collecting spatial coordinates and localized SPPs at the lattice site A, the real-space pattern of ‘N-U-A-A’ array (Fig. 4b) appears, and there exist no obvious SPP crosstalk between adjacent Kekulé structures. We further compared the normalized optical field intensity distribution data (see SI Fig. S13 for details), where the intensity of central lattice site A collected from M=4 structure is four times than that for M=0 one, consistent with the measured intensity ratio from two independent structures. Noted that scattering mechanism may occur and emit light out from the basal gold plane, once the thickness of gold film surpasses 70 nm due to limited leakage transmission. The conceptual validation of out-of-plane light-emitting arrays is displayed in SI Fig. S12. In addition, the on-chip planar Kekulé arrays exhibit similar optical lattices and ‘N-U-A-A’ emission pattern even under broad white light irradiation (please see SI Fig. S16), indicating their appropriateness as broadband nano-lenser arrays, at a wafer-scale levels.

In-plane SPP lattices for imaging encryption/decryption
The variable SPP lattices with multiple DOFs are potentially detached channels for in-plane imaging encryption36. We propose an encryption/decryption scheme by employing an in-plane Kekulé metasurface under RCP incident light (Fig. 5a), and the image information stored in different encryption channels of co-polarized (RCP) and cross-polarized (LCP) analyzers, which behaved as the keys. When the LCP analyzer is the key, a binary Cameraman cover image is constructed (Fig. 5b), which can be recognized as a matrix A a×b (a=b=256) with values of 0 and 1, corresponding to black and white in the targeted cameraman binary image, respectively. Here, we encrypted two stable in-plane hexagonal and honeycomb lattices (Fig. 5c) as 1 and 0, respectively.

With the RCP analyzer as the other key, a Couple gray cover image is encrypted and each pixel intensity value is fitted for a gray scale ranging from 0 to 255 (Fig. 5d). Different from aforementioned LCP channel, we employed the widely continuously tunable amplitude of lattice site A as another matrix A R a×b (a=b=512) with 0 to 255 different values according to its brightness. Afterwards, this Couple image could be decoded into a series of binary images based on the conversion between decimal and binary (Fig. 5e), and in our scheme, two cipher binary images of the logo of Chinese characters of ‘南京航空航天大学‘ (360 pixels×360 pixels, Fig. 5f) and letters of ‘NUAA’ (181 pixels×70 pixels, Fig. 5g) are stored in the 0th and 1st of the least significant bit (LSB) of upper left corner of Couple cover image (details see SI section S17). Such anti-counterfeiting process by encrypting and decrypting is based on in-plane optical SPP lattices rather than reflected or transmitted light in conventional optical encryption with metasurfaces36.

---

## Methods

Sample fabrication
Using an electron-beam evaporation system (Syskey E-Beam Evaporation system), 5nm thick Ti (serving as an adhesion layer, deposition rate of 0.5Å/s) and 50nm (200nm) thick Au layers (deposition rate of 2Å/s) were sequentially deposited on a quartz substrate or a PET film. Afterward, Kekulé structures were precisely milled within Ti/Au film using a FEI Helios G4 UX focused ion beam (FIB) system. The FIB milling parameters were set to: voltage of 30 kV and current of 7 pA. Under a scanning electron microscope, the uniform geometry of nanoslits-the building block of Kekulé structure-is confirmed to be ~230 nm in length and ~118 nm in width. The processing field for the array is 50 μm, with a processing time of approximately 2 minutes. When processing a small field (such as 7 μm), the processing time for a single Kekulé metasurface structure is approximately 10 seconds.

Optical characterization
Using an inverted optical microscope (NanoWizard Sense) with an oil immersion objective lens (100× magnification, NA=1.30), the leakage radiation from the underside of the sample was collected. The collected radiation was then directed through a custom-built optical path (the signal was further processed via a filter and mask), and finally imaged using a CCD camera (Princeton Instrument PIXIS 1024) for real-space and Fourier-plane imaging. The detailed design optical path is shown in SI Fig. S8.

Numerical simulations
Full-wave numerical simulations were performed using the finite-different time-domain (FDTD) technique. A single nanoslit unit cell in 50nm-thick gold film was adopted. The incident wave was polarized along x- or y-axes and illuminated the nanoslits from the substrate side. Along x- and y-axes, periodic boundary conditions were applied, and a perfectly matched layer (PML) boundary condition was used along the z direction. The polarization conversion efficiency (PCE) is obtained as a function of nanoslit length L and width W at a wavelength of 633 nm (see Supplementary Fig. S2) by sweeping these values between 50 nm and 250 nm with an interval of 5 nm.

Data availability
All data needed to evaluate the conclusions in the paper are present in the paper or the Supplementary Materials. The materials that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this work, the authors studied the interference of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) into periodic patterns in a metal film by arranging nanoslits into a Kekulé pattern. By adding additional nanoslits in a wing-shaped configuration, the authors observed transformations in the patterns, particularly a brighter central spot. They further utilized this design for various applications, such as configurable optical arrays and optical encryption.
However, my main concern with this work is the appropriateness of using the term “Wigner crystal” to describe the optical phenomenon observed. A Wigner crystal typically refers to periodic patterns formed by electron-electron interactions, such as Coulomb repulsive forces. In this study, the pattern is formed purely by interference, and the system is linear, with no interactions between photons. Therefore, the analogy of the photonic system to a Wigner crystal does not seem valid. Indeed, the use of terminologies such as “melt into” and “SPP crystallization” in the abstract and throughout the main text appears to be an overreach.
In my opinion, the concept of an optical Wigner crystal presented in this work is fundamentally flawed. Moreover, there is already a substantial body of research on using geometric phases to manipulate the interference patterns of SPP waves on 2D metallic platforms. Based on these considerations, I do not recommend the publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 2

The paper presents an innovative contribution to the field of plasmonics and nanophotonics by introducing a novel Kekulé metasurface platform for creating optical Wigner crystal (WC) lattices. The concept of extending Wigner crystals from electrons to photons is very interesting. It opens new avenues for exploring quantum phenomena in photonic systems. The design of the Kekulé metasurface, with its head-to-tail arrangement of nanoslits, is well-conceived and allows for precise control over the spatial distribution and relative intensity of WC lattice sites. The ability to tailor these properties by superposing extra wing-shaped nanoslits is particularly impressive, offering a high degree of tunability. The experimental validation of the theoretical predictions is robust, with leakage radiation microscopy (LRM) providing clear visualization of the optical WC lattices. The alignment between experimental results and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations further underscores the reliability of the proposed platform.
The paper could benefit from addressing several limitations and providing more detailed analyses.
One notable omission is a thorough discussion of surface plasmon polariton (SPP) decay and losses. SPPs are known to suffer from significant propagation losses due to Ohmic damping in metals, which could limit the practical applications of the proposed platform. A more in-depth exploration of how the Kekulé metasurface mitigates these losses, or how they impact the performance of the optical WC lattices, would strengthen the paper. For instance, the authors could investigate the use of low-loss materials like silver or alternative plasmonic materials to enhance performance.
Additionally, the paper does not mention the scalability of the Kekulé metasurface for large-scale integration. The fabrication of such precise nanostructures, particularly with the addition of wing-shaped nanoslits, could pose significant challenges and may limit practical implementation. Providing more details on the fabrication process, including potential challenges and strategies for scaling up production, would be valuable.
On the other hand, it would be useful to see the quantitative metrics for evaluating the performance of the demonstrated applications. For example, the quantification of the efficiency of the light-emitting arrays and the security level of the image encryption scheme. Understanding this is the early stage of the technology, maybe an analysis of the potential would be sufficient. This would be helpful to assess their practical viability compared to existing technologies.
Finally, it would be good to see more details on the theoretical framework for the formation of optical WC lattices, the mathematical treatment could be more rigorous. Expanding the derivation of the in-plane electric field (Equation 1) to include more detailed explanations of the underlying assumptions and approximations, as well as a deeper discussion of the physical mechanisms governing the formation and melting of the optical WC lattices, would enhance the theoretical depth of the study.

Comment 1: However, my main concern with this work is the appropriateness of using the
term “Wigner crystal” to describe the optical phenomenon observed. A Wigner crystal typically

forces. In this study, the pattern is formed purely by interference, and the system is linear, with
no interactions between photons. Therefore, the analogy of the photonic system to a Wigner
crystal does not seem valid. Indeed, the use of terminologies such as “melt into” and “SPP

Reply #1: We sincerely thank you and understand your concern. Surface plasmon polaritons
(SPPs) exhibit both wave and particle properties[ Nat. Phys. 5, 470-474, (2009)], therefore,
numerous envisions emerge attempting to elucidate the formation and evolution SPPs from the
view of quasiparticles[ Nat. Rev. Phys. 2, 538-561, (2020)], exactly as what we try in this study.
By patterning polygonal metasurface with hexagonal symmetry, several plasmonic lattices are
reported, such as optical skyrmion lattice[ Science 361, 993-996, (2018)] and hexagonal
lattice[ Sci. Adv. 11, eadv3938, (2025)]. However, tuning the 2D topography and relative
intensity of these plasmonic lattices remains challenging. To tackle these limitations, we
developed a Kekulé metasurface featured with (1) nanoslits in head-to-tail fashion assembled
into regular hexagon nanostructures, (2) benzene-type hexagon with alternatively neighboring
structures and (3) extra wing-shaped nanoslit sets, and elegantly realize the spatial control of
SPPs with numerous degrees of freedom (DOFs), analogous to kaleidoscopic electron
localization behaviors in 2D electron systems. As you pointed out, however, the expression of
“Optical Wigner Crystal” is inappropriate and immature at present stages. In this concern, the
“Optical Wigner Crystal lattices” has been carefully revised to “Optical Wigner-type lattices”,
and some misleading expression including “melt into” and “SPP crystallization” was removed,
for the sake of appropriateness. The usage of “Wigner-type” is to visually describe the lattice
pattern with tunable topography, and hopefully attempt to inspire more investigations of 2D
SPPs as (quasi-)particles. Below is our detailed interpretation from five essential aspects:
1) Generalized Wigner lattice beyond traditional electron landscape: The classical
“Wigner crystal”, first predicted by Eugene Wigner in 1934, describes the periodic patterns of
electrons under certain electron-electron interactions. More recently, however, a variety of
generalized Wigner crystals were reported and categorized in the following Table R1. As a
supplement to the classical electron system, generalized Wigner crystals (WCs) have been
successionally demonstrated in Moiré superlattice systems (for holes) and even molecular
ensembles. These generalized WCs typically arises from the synergistic interplay between
the Moiré potential confinement and long-range Coulomb interactions among
quasiparticles. In addition, WCs were also reported in cold atomic/ionic systems through
engineered approaches such as Feshbach resonance, optical lattice confinement, dipolar
interaction modulation, and ion trap potentials. It is noteworthy that, particularly in cold atomic
systems, the intrinsic interatomic interactions (dominated by van der Waals forces) are
extremely weak and only become significant at ultralow interatomic distances. These
natural interactions are far insufficient to overcome quantum or thermal fluctuations to induce
spontaneous spatial ordering. Without engineered strategies to (i) enhance repulsive
interactions, (ii) suppress kinetic energy, and (iii) tailor geometric configurations, Wigner
crystallization cannot emerge spontaneously. These studies stand in stark contrast to
conventional electron systems, where WCs form spontaneously due to the naturally dominant
long-range Coulomb interactions. In our work, we utilize Kekulé design to "customize" the
boundary conditions of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs), achieving periodic modulation of
SPP fields. This approach shares conceptual similarities with engineered potential design in
cold atomic systems: both relying on artificially designed potentials (e.g., optical lattices or
nanostructures) to break natural symmetry and establish functional periodicity.
Table R1. Generalized Wigner crystals reported in literatures.
2) SPPs as quasiparticles. Numerous theoretical and experimental studies have confirmed the
quasiparticle behavior of SPPs[ Nat. Phys. 5, 470-474, (2009); Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 719-722,
(2013); Nature 450, 402-406, (2007); Phys. Rev. Appl. 2, 014004, (2014)]. Among these, Dheur
M C et al. pioneerly demonstrated the wave-particle duality for a single SPP freely propagating
along a planar metal-air interface[ Sci. Adv. 2, e1501574, (2016)]. Stimulated by these, we re-
consider 2D SPPs more from the quasiparticle perspective, which involves designing Kekulé
nanostructures to regulate the momentum of SPPs, thereby achieving efficient quasiparticle
wavefunction superposition. Given the absence of many-body interactions among SPP
quasiparticles here, we replaced "Wigner crystal lattice" by "Wigner-type lattice" to
emphasize structural WCs analogy while distinguishing it from traditional systems
dominated by Coulomb interactions.
3) Theoretical Commonalities between electronic Wigner Crystals and plasmonic system.
Schulz H J et al. provided a unified theoretical framework for Wigner Crystal in one
dimension[ Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 1864, (1993)]. In such framework, plasmon and spin excitations
in one-dimensional structures is somehow consistent and the electron arrangement rules may
also suitable for collective oscillation of electrons (e.g. SPPs). This suggests the feasibility
of extending the WC lattice over SPPs but in a broader way. Thus, "Wigner-type lattice" is
adopted here to capture and present SPPs behavior as plasmonic quasiparticles, similar to what
Wigner Crystals lattice to electron and its analogs.
4) Electronic-to-photonic conceptual migration. The cross-disciplinary migration of
scientific concepts is exemplified by the cases such as the extension of "optical skyrmions"
concept from non-linear nuclear physics, spintronics to photonics via several studies upon
linear plasmonics[Phys. Rev. Lett. 87, 037203, (2001); Science 341, 636-639, (2013); Science
361, 993-996, (2018)]. To be specified, the concept of Skyrmions was initially proposed by
Tony Skyrme[Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences 260, 127-138, (1961)]and
represents topological manifestations of strongly interacting matter in nuclear physics,
fundamentally relying on non-perturbative QCD effects. Later in emerging spintronic
technologies, two-dimensional magnetic Skyrmions, as topological spin textures, emerge from
the synergistic interplay of multiple magnetic exchange interactions (e.g., Heisenberg
exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, etc.). In contrast, optical Skyrmions were first
theoretically proposed and experimentally realized by Tsesses S et al. in 2018[ Science 361,
993-996, (2018)]. The formation of optical Skyrmions relies entirely on evanescent field
manipulation within linear plasmonic systems, without requiring SPPs interactions.
Although their formation mechanisms and physical origins differ significantly from those in
nuclear physics and spintronic systems (non-linear to linear evolution), the extension of
Skyrmions into photonic systems opens up diverse possibilities in photonics, including optical
information processing, transmissions, and storages.
Another familiar example is the concept of "photonic crystals", which is borrowed
from semiconductor band theory in solid-state physics. Unlike the periodic Coulomb potentials
in atomic lattices, photonic crystals utilize designed periodic dielectric constant distributions as
effective potentials. In addition, electronic bandgaps arise from destructive interference of
electron wavefunctions in periodic potentials, whereas photonic bandgaps result from Bragg
scattering-induced destructive interference of light in dielectric structures[ Phys. Rev. Lett. 58,
2059, (1987)]. This seemingly unrelated concept between its electronic and photonic
counterpart triggers many impressive progresses and promotes the adoption of "Wigner-type
lattice" to describe the periodic photonic pattern in this study.
5) Research highlights of our work. Linear plasmonic systems holds significant scientific
interests. For instance, Tsesses S et al. recently employed geometric phase to design plasmonic
quasi-crystalline structures, and established the intrinsic connection between global symmetry
and topological properties in two-dimensional plasmonic quasicrystals[ Science 387, 644-648,
(2025)]. In another study, Schwab J et al. utilized geometric phase to engineer Morse soliton
superlattice structures and explored dual electronic paradigms in plasmonic systems with non-
trivial topology[ Nat. Phys., 1-7, (2025)]. These works collectively underscore the broad
research and application potential of linear plasmonic systems.
In the scope of linear plasmonic systems, we proposed and demonstrated how the Kekulé-type
metasurfaces become new controllable and abundant degrees of freedom for engineering
potential fields toward configurable optical arrays and optical encryption. The key message in
this work lies in four aspects:
a) The plasmonic lattice based on Kekulé structures exhibits unique orbital angular
momentum, under different combination of polarization states of incident and detected
lights, leading to the topographic evolution of distinct Wigner-type lattices.
b) Adjusting the number and positions of extra wing-shaped nanoslits over the Kekulé
structure cumulatively alters the intensity and morphology of in-plane lattice sites, in a
precisely controlled way.
c) The high-fidelity Wigner-type lattice demonstrates broadband characteristics,
maintaining its properties even under white light excitation. In addition, this Wigner-
type lattices well retains although the Kekulé metasurface is scaled down to 2 µm. This
broadband feature without crosstalk showcasing the potential of Kekulé metasurface
for miniaturized plasmonic integrated circuits.
d) We demonstrate that optical Wigner-type lattices with amplitude-amplified lattice sites
can be applied as configurable on-chip light-emitting arrays and image
encryption/decryption systems, thereby enriching the family of metasurfaces for
advanced nanolasers and information security applications.
In conclusion, the novelty of our work lies in the designed Kekulé metasurfaces, extra wing-
shaped nanoslits and their corresponding modulations over plasmonic lattices, accompanied by
their use in configurable light-emitting arrays and image encryption/decryption. To avoid any
inappropriateness or misleading caused upon as-manifested SPPs pattern, the expression of
"Wigner Crystal lattice" was replaced by “Wiger-type lattice” to describe these periodic
plasmonic lattice pattern akin to conventional and generalized electronic ones.

(b): Our encryption scheme analysis: In our encryption scheme, the hidden information is
first embedded into the least significant bit (LSB) and then second least significant bit of the
cover image using LSB steganography. The cover image is a 512×512-pixel grayscale image.
The speckle information is then encoded into a Kekulé metasurface structure array using optical
wavelength and polarization state (e.g., RCP) as the key. Our work achieves dual-channel
metasurface keys, where the binary image in the LCP channel can serve as a key to interact
with the hidden information in the RCP channel. The transformation pattern of cover image
and interaction rules can also be encoded into the metasurface. For the decryption, authorized
users must use the wavelength/polarization key to obtain the LCP-channel key and speckle
information. The cover image is restored and transformed to obtain the hidden image, which is
then decrypted using the LCP-channel key[ Nat. Commun. 15, 2607, (2024); Sci. Adv. 7,
eabg0363, (2021)].
Additionally, we conducted quantitative evaluations of the LSB steganography employed in
our encryption scheme. Through discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and histogram distribution
analyses comparing the original cover image and the encrypted cover image, we observed that
both images exhibit nearly identical global frequency distributions in their magnitude spectra
(Figure R2-5f-h), with stable low-frequency energy concentration (mean difference <0.5% in
logarithmic magnitude values). This confirms that the encryption process preserves the original
structural integrity while enhancing resistance against frequency-domain attacks through pixel-
level perturbations—spectral discrepancies cannot be exploited for reverse engineering.
Furthermore, the histograms of the original and encrypted cover images demonstrate
statistically similar distributions (Figure R2-5i-k): the mean intensity remains nearly unchanged
(original: 123.18 vs. encrypted: 123.31–123.35), the standard deviation stays stable (≈40.06–
40.07), and overlapping probability density curves validate the unaltered global intensity
distribution. These results indicate that the algorithm effectively conceals local pixel
correlations without introducing detectable statistical anomalies, thereby thwarting histogram-
based cryptanalysis.
